bib.title: IntelliCode Compose: Code Generation using Transformer
bib.venue: ESEC/FSE '20 (28th ACM Joint European Software Engineering Conference and Symposium on the Foundations of Software Engineering)

question: Can a GPT-2-style transformer trained from scratch on multilingual source code complete whole lines of code fast enough (under 100 ms) for IDE use?
hypothesis: A generative transformer pretrained on raw code tokens, without static-analysis features, can infer identifier types and long-range semantics well enough to complete up to whole lines.
contributions: GPT-C: a GPT-2 variant trained from scratch on a large multilingual code corpus, compared with monolingual versions and an n-gram baseline
IntelliCode Compose: an end-to-end deployed completion system with GPT-C and client-side caching
Evaluation of pretraining quality by perplexity (1.82 best) and of completion by edit similarity (86.7%)
MultiGPT-C: a multilingual model and a comparison of four multilingual modelling approaches
Documentation of practical challenges of training intermediate-sized transformers on HPC clusters and deploying in the cloud

method.summary: GPT-C, a decoder-only GPT-2 variant (tied embeddings), is pretrained from scratch on 1.2B lines of Python, C#, JavaScript and TypeScript with a sentencepiece BPE subtoken vocabulary and literal/comment normalisation. It is served from a cloud service with batched beam search, key/value caching, ONNX graph optimisations and a client-side trie cache.
method.task: next-token code language modelling for line-level code completion

datasets.name: GitHub multilingual code corpus (C#, Python, JavaScript, TypeScript)
datasets.size: over 1.2 billion lines of source code; over 52000 top-starred non-fork projects; over 4.7 million files (C# 1172k files/201M lines/4836 repos; Python 1200k/240M/18174; JavaScript 1982k/681M/26553; TypeScript 437k/85M/3255)
datasets.split: 70-30 dev/test at repository level; dev split at random 80-20 into train/validation; final deployed model retrained on the entire dataset
datasets.source: top-starred GitHub projects; licence not stated
datasets.preprocessing: Lexer-token stream; code regenerated in common style; subtokens via sentencepiece (BPE); special tokens <BOF>, <EOF>, <EOL>, <INDENT>, <DEDENT>; numeric/string literals and comments replaced by <NUM_LIT>, <STR_LIT>, <COMMENT> (also <CHAR_LIT> for C#, <RE_LIT> for JS), keeping top frequent literals as <STR_LIT:lit> (Table 2: Python 200 strings/50 numbers; kept literals represent 18%/63% for Python, 13%/58% C#, 20%/70% JS,TS in the table order as printed)

models.name: GPT-C (monolingual)
models.architecture: decoder-only transformer (GPT-2 variant), output layer tied to input embedding with projection matrix

models.name: MultiGPT-C (double heads)
models.architecture: GPT-C with LM head plus multiple-choice language-classification head

other.note: Table 3 calls the multilingual model 24-layer while section 6 says best multilingual has 26 layers

models.name: DistilGPT-C tiny / small
models.init_from: pretrained teacher weights and biases (26-layer teacher)

training.objective: autoregressive log-likelihood, categorical cross-entropy; MultiGPT-C adds multiple-choice language classification
training.lr_schedule: learning rate decay of 0.98 per epoch; also described as cosine decay per epoch
training.warmup: increased during the first few epochs (length not stated)
training.hardware: 5 Lambda V100 boxes, each sixteen V100 32GB GPUs; 80 GPU workers for Table 3; Horovod with Adasum, PyTorch 1.2.0, CUDA 10, Kubernetes
training.wall_clock: 2.8 hours per epoch monolingual, 19.7 hours per epoch multilingual (80 GPUs)

other.batch_size_inconsistency: text says 128, Table 3 says cumulative batch size 160
other.multilingual_batching: each mini-batch drawn from a single language sampled at random
other.throughput: 163 +- 5 samples/s and 167000 +- 5000 tokens/s monolingual; 148 +- 5 and 152000 +- 5000 multilingual

inference.decoding: beam search over subtokens, batched candidates (L inference calls rather than L x k), cached attention keys/values; stops at preset subtoken count or break token (<EOL> etc.)
inference.prompting: code context only; multilingual control-code variant prefixes 'lang *'

other.server: Azure Kubernetes Service, Python, PyTorch and ONNX runtime with constant folding and fused LayerNorm/GELU

metrics.name: Perplexity
metrics.definition: exp of cross-entropy on test tokens (Eq. 12)

metrics.name: ROUGE-L precision/recall
metrics.definition: longest-common-subsequence overlap between suggestion and target

metrics.name: Edit similarity
metrics.definition: Levenshtein-based similarity between suggested and target sequence

metrics.name: Syntactic correctness
metrics.definition: fraction of suggestions that tree-sitter parses with file context (EOL removed from break tokens, Black used to flatten)

metrics.name: Surfacing rate (SR)
metrics.definition: completions displayed / times a completion could be shown (after every character)

eval.protocol: Held-out test set split by repository; single run, no seeds or significance tests; online telemetry over >150 thousand requests.

availability.code: not released (proprietary; Horovod Adasum PR linked)

limits: No statistical tests, seeds or variance for model metrics; single training runs.
Offline metrics are string similarity, not functional correctness; online CTR only 10% and measured only on an internal rollout.
Hyperparameter search, total training tokens/steps/epochs and compute cost are not reported.
Dataset licences and the literal-keep percentages are only in a garbled Table 2; model and code not released.
Internal inconsistencies: batch size 128 vs 160; multilingual 26 vs 24 layers; 355M GPT-2 baseline not code-trained.
Authors concede syntax failures partly from partial statements and that SR is systematically understated by typing momentum.
Dated: GPT-2-scale model, pre-Codex; no functional-correctness benchmarks such as HumanEval.
